q-113668.name: Question 1
q-113668.worked_solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We apply the power rule with $n=13$, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{13}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{13+1}}{13+1}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{14}}{14}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{14}}{14}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{14}}{14})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{1}{14}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{14})+0 & = \\ \frac{1}{14}\cdot 14\,{x}^{13} & = \\ {x}^{13}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

q-29994.worked_solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We apply the power rule with $n=4$, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{4+1}}{4+1}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{5}}{5})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{1}{5}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{5})+0 & = \\ \frac{1}{5}\cdot 5{x}^{4} & = \\ {x}^{4}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

q-2024.name: Question 4
q-2024.worked_solution:
We start by writing the root as a rational power, $\sqrt{x}={x}^{1/2}.$ So, we can apply the power rule with $n=\frac{1}{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{1/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{1/2+1}}{(\frac{1}{2}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3/2}}{(\frac{3}{2})}+C \\  & =\frac{2{x}^{3/2}}{3}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2{x}^{3/2}}{3}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2{x}^{3/2}}{3})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{2}{3}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3/2})+0 & = \\ \frac{2}{3}\cdot \frac{3}{2}{x}^{3/2-1} & = \\ {x}^{1/2}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

q-29665.name: Question 5
q-29665.worked_solution:
We start by writing the root as a rational power, $\sqrt{{x}^{3}}={x}^{3/2}.$ So, we can apply the power rule with $n=\frac{3}{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \sqrt{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{3/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3/2+1}}{(\frac{3}{2}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{5/2}}{(\frac{5}{2})}+C \\  & =\frac{2{x}^{5/2}}{5}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, let's check by differentiating:

$$

Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{-3/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-3/2+1}}{(-\frac{3}{2}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-1/2}}{(-\frac{1}{2})}+C \\  & =-2{x}^{-1/2}+C \\  & =-\frac{2}{{x}^{1/2}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

q-29993.worked_solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}={x}^{-3/2}.$ So, we can use the power rule with $n=-\frac{3}{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{-3/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-3/2+1}}{(-\frac{3}{2}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-1/2}}{(-\frac{1}{2})}+C \\  & =-2{x}^{-1/2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$
